titre: “God Is Dead”: A Madman, a Lantern, and No One to Understand
accroche: In The Gay Science (1882), the phrase is not an atheist's slogan: it is shouted by a madman, in a marketplace, before unbelievers who laugh.
contenu_vulgarise:
“God is dead — Nietzsche.” The phrase circulates as graffiti, as a magazine cover, as a line in a term paper, as if the philosopher had announced the victory of atheism over religion. But you have to go back to the page, in *The Gay Science* (1882), to paragraph 125, titled “The Insane Man” or “The Madman” depending on the translation. The scene is not the one people think it is.

## The Scene

On a bright morning, a man lights a lantern, runs into the marketplace, and cries out without letup: “I seek God!” Around him, many people do not believe in God, and his agitation amuses them: Is he lost? Is he hiding? Has he gone to sea, has he emigrated? The madman leaps into their midst and pierces them with his gaze: “We have killed him, you and I! We are all his murderers.” Then his questions pour out: how did we drink up the sea, wipe away the horizon, unchain the earth from its sun? Isn't it colder now? Isn't night continually closing in? He asks how we will console ourselves, what atonements we will invent, and whether the greatness of the deed is not too great for its authors.

No one answers. The madman throws his lantern to the ground, where it breaks, and says: “I come too early. This prodigious event is still on its way; it has not yet reached the ears of men.” He then enters several churches to sing a requiem for God there, and answers those who throw him out: what are these churches now, if not the tombs and funeral monuments of God?

## Who Speaks, and to Whom

The madman's listeners are unbelievers: they are the ones laughing. The madman does not congratulate them for having stopped believing; he reproaches them for not measuring what that entails. The finding is not “God does not exist,” but “what held Europe together — morality, meaning, orientation — held together by this belief, and no one has yet drawn the consequence of its collapse.”

The phrase is not Nietzsche's own, moreover: it circulated before him, notably in a 17th-century Lutheran hymn and in a 1797 novel by Jean Paul, which Hegel had also taken up in a very different sense. What he brings that is new is the register: not an atheist's joy, but the vertigo of someone who has just realized that there is no longer any up or down. A text that people cite to close a discussion opens, when reread, onto anxiety: what do we put in its place?

repere.texte: In The Gay Science (1882), aphorism 125, the madman who announces the death of God addresses people who “did not believe in God”; his lantern broken, he concludes: “I come too early” (translation by Thomas Common, 1910). The phrase appears before Nietzsche, notably in Jean Paul (Siebenkäs, 1797).
repere.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Die fröhliche Wissenschaft, 1882, §125; English trans. Thomas Common, The Joyful Wisdom, 1910 (Project Gutenberg)

carte.punch: “God is dead”: Nietzsche puts it in the mouth of a madman, before unbelievers who laugh.
carte.idee: In The Gay Science (1882, §125), the madman cries “we have killed him” to people who no longer believe. He does not congratulate them: he tells them they have not measured what this changes, and concludes “I come too early.”

quiz.question: To whom does the madman of The Gay Science (§125) announce the death of God, and how does he react to them?
choix: Unbelievers who laugh at him; he reproaches them for not grasping the scope of the event
Scandalized believers; he congratulates them on their faithfulness
Scholars gathered in an academy; he asks them to publish proof that God does not exist
Children in the square; he explains atheism to them in simple terms
quiz.explication: The text specifies that the people around him did not believe in God: the madman proves nothing, he reproaches them for not measuring what their own unbelief implies. There are no believers to reassure, no academy, and no lesson in atheism.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the madman do with his lantern at the end of the scene?
choix: He hands it to a passerby and asks him to carry on
He throws it to the ground, where it breaks, saying he comes too early
He carefully puts it out and goes home without a word
He sets it down at the threshold of a church before going in
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Getting no answer, the madman throws his lantern, which breaks, and says “I come too early”: the event has not yet reached the ears of men.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the madman answer to those who throw him out of the churches?
choix: That these churches are the tombs and funeral monuments of God
That these churches must be rebuilt in order to find God there
That these churches are the only places where God still lives
That these churches will soon be empty, for lack of worshippers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After singing a requiem for God, the madman answers that the churches are now nothing but tombs and funeral monuments of God.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the entry say about the origin of the phrase “God is dead”?
choix: Nietzsche invents it in 1882 in this paragraph of The Gay Science
Voltaire launches it in the 18th century against the Catholic Church
It circulated before Nietzsche, notably in Jean Paul in 1797
Marx utters it in 1848 in a text on religion
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The phrase appears before Nietzsche, in a 17th-century Lutheran hymn and in Jean Paul in 1797; what is new is its register of vertigo.
